paper.authors_full: Lucas Memmert, Izabel Cvetkovic, Navid Tavanapour, Eva Bittner
paper.title: Brainstorming with a Generative Language Model: Effect of Exposure to AI Ideas on Brainstorming Performance and Cognitive Load
paper.pdf_filename: Memmert et al (2025) - Brainstorming with a Generative Language Model.pdf
paper.version_read: Published journal version of record: Business & Information Systems Engineering 68(5):1023–1047 (2026); published online 18 November 2025; DOI 10.1007/s12599-025-00974-y (PDF p. 1, printed p. 1023).
paper.one_line_finding: With on-demand GPT-3.5 ideas, participants' final idea lists (own plus copied GLM ideas) were longer (mdn 7 vs 5; U = 963.5, p = 0.006) and covered more categories (mdn 5 vs 3; U = 1080.0, p < 0.001), and their shortlists were rated more novel (mean 3.396 vs 2.876; t(73) = 2.889, p = 0.005, d = 0.667) and more valuable (mdn 4.900 vs 4.425; U = 994.0, p = 0.002), but they wrote fewer ideas themselves (mdn 4 vs 5; U = 475.0, text p = 0.015; Fig. 7a instead marks **, defined as p < .01) and their own ideas were not rated more novel (U = 699.5, p = 0.406) or valuable (U = 737.5, p = 0.204) (PDF pp. 12-13, Sects. 4.1-4.2, Figs. 7-8).
paper.shared_samples: Possible overlap with Memmert and Bittner (2024, HICSS-57; c861). The c861 source says it reanalyzes an unnamed previous study under review and reports 52 analyzed participants (26 per arm). Identical participant quotations appear in c861 and c098 under different participant IDs: the quote below is attributed to c861 P29 and c098 P74, and the passage beginning "It felt a lot faster" to c861 P52 and c098 P48. These matches support possible shared data, but neither source establishes the identity or number of overlapping quantitative participants. c098 cites c861 and Memmert (2024, ECIS) as prior work without declaring sample overlap. Independence remains unconfirmed; obtain author confirmation before assigning independent sample IDs.

studies.label: Between-subjects brainstorming experiment: human-only vs human + GLM (food waste)

counts_source.quote: Of the remaining 75 participants (age: mean = 23.3, min = 18, max = 37 years; gender: 13 female, 62 male), all but one are in study programs at the informatics department.

arms.name: human + GLM
arms.description: Individual brainstorming in the purpose-built app with its GLM function active. Participants request suggestions using a fixed-prompt Generate ideas button and may copy, edit, or ignore them; at least one request was required (PDF pp. 9-10, printed pp. 1031-1032, Sects. 3.2-3.3).

arms.name: human-only
arms.description: Individual brainstorming in the same app with its GLM function deactivated (PDF p. 9, printed p. 1031, Sect. 3.2).

studies.task: Brainstorm for 10 minutes on “How can we reduce food waste?”, then select the four best ideas from the long list (PDF p. 8, printed p. 1030, Sect. 3.1; PDF p. 11, printed p. 1033, Sect. 3.5).

ai_tool.name: OpenAI GPT-3.5-turbo-0301 (temperature 0.9), embedded in the brainstorming app
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 9 (printed p. 1031), Sect. 3.3; model and temperature explicitly named, model release year not stated

studies.shared_sample: The screening form flags possible overlap with Memmert and Bittner (2024; c861), based on matching participant quotations and c861's statement that it reanalyzes a previous study, and flags related ECIS reports. The present paper cites these reports without declaring shared participants. The identity and number of overlapping quantitative participants remain unconfirmed; do not assume independent samples. Source: forms/c098.json, sample_overlap; the matching quotation in this paper is on PDF p. 15 (printed p. 1037), Sect. 4.4.1.

estimates.notes: This robustness outcome counts qualifying ideas, so it is coded as fluency/category_count; its form_outcome_id links to the screening form's novelty or value outcome under which the robustness analysis is described. Threshold quotation (PDF p. 13, printed p. 1035, Sect. 4.1): “above average ideas for novelty (mean = 3.396) and value (mean = 4.747), respectively, in the long-lists of ideas.” n_total uses the printed common analytic sample in Sect. 3.4. open_items: The number randomized and labeled per-arm analyzed counts are not printed. Sect. 3.4 (PDF p. 10, printed p. 1032) reports 77 completers and two exclusions, with 75 remaining participants. Sect. 3.6 (PDF p. 12, printed p. 1034) gives unlabeled group sizes of 38 and 37; these cannot be assigned to named arms. For human-level shortlist quality, four treated participants were excluded, but the resulting analysis total is not printed; the GPT-4 shortlist analyses also have no explicit final count. Those estimate counts remain null. Long-list Good-Idea-Count records use the printed common analytic sample, because the outcome is explicitly independent of shortlist selection and no additional long-list exclusions are stated; robustness-specific counts are not repeated beside the tests.

Participant-level arm SDs, SEs, and numerical confidence limits are absent. Only human-judge dyad novelty has printed arm means. The interval type and endpoints in Fig. 8c (PDF p. 13, printed p. 1035) are not stated; no statistics were digitized or derived.
Human-fluency significance conflicts: Sect. 4.1 prints p = 0.015, while Fig. 7a uses ** with caption **p < .01 (PDF pp. 12-13, printed pp. 1034-1035). The text value is retained.

For human fluency the paper prints a negative rank-biserial correlation but a positive converted Cohen’s d; no conversion formula or SD denominator is specified. The standardizer for the human-judge dyad novelty Cohen’s d is also not defined (PDF pp. 12-13, printed pp. 1034-1035).

The Good-Idea-Count novelty threshold is printed as 3.396 in Sect. 4.1 and the same number is printed as the treated dyad-level human-judge novelty mean in Sect. 4.2 (PDF p. 13, printed p. 1035). Supplement 12599_2025_974_MOESM1_ESM.pdf, PDF p. 6 (printed p. 4), Appendix D, Table D.1, defines the threshold as the average GPT-4 novelty rating across long lists from all sessions, but prints no numerical cutoff and does not explain the duplicated value. Author clarification remains necessary; no correction was made.

The screening form flags possible participant overlap with c861 and a related ECIS paper; the present paper does not establish the overlapping participants. Independent sample IDs require reconciliation.
The paper does not designate human-level or dyad-level novelty as primary and reports no preregistration. Selection between the two human-judge novelty records remains an Atlas decision.

The experiment took place in university seminars; whether the task was ordinary coursework and explicitly supervised is not stated. lab_rct follows the standardized experimental task and the reconciled form. Only a Western European university is specified for the participants, so no country was inferred from author affiliations.
The exact assistance model is named, but its release year and the data-collection dates are not explicitly stated in the paper. ai_tool.year remains null.
